Equiloc Quad 2Tri

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: join the middle points of a four-sided shape with two equal sides and the new shape always has four equal sides.
How to play: Drag S around the circle, or C and D along the sloping lines. Tick the boxes to show point names, the joining lines or a hint; you can also focus a point and use the arrow keys.
Look for the math

This old page still embeds the Java applet. Its diagram takes the midpoints of a four-sided shape whose sides AD and BC are equal, and draws a new four-sided shape KMLN inside. No matter how you drag the points, the new shape has four equal sides. The old article prints the midpoint list incorrectly; this page follows the applet's own code, as does the logic test.

Midlines of triangles

Join the midpoints of two sides of a triangle and the new segment is parallel to the third side and half as long — the midpoint theorem. The applet puts K at the midpoint of AC, L at that of BD, M at that of AB, and N at that of CD. So in triangle ABC, KM is half of BC; in triangle ABD, ML is half of AD; in triangle BCD, LN is half of BC; and in triangle ACD, NK is half of AD.

Why it is a rhombus

Because AD = BC, all four of those halves are the same length, and the pairs are parallel to the same two lines. A quadrilateral with four equal sides and opposite sides parallel is a rhombus. The logic test checks this on thousands of dragged pictures and on 2,000 other four-sided shapes drawn at random with AD = BC: no exception. The angle between the two sides need not be 60 degrees; the random cases include many other angles.

Where the sixty degrees come from

A, B and S lie on one circle, and the arc from A to B is 120 degrees, so the angle at S where the two equal sides meet is 60 degrees (or 120 on the other arc). The rhombus then has a short diagonal that cuts it into two equilateral triangles. At the start that diagonal is KL: triangles KML and KNL are equilateral. On the other arc the short diagonal is MN instead. The circle keeps the line angle at 60 degrees here; to see a rhombus at another angle, use a different four-sided shape.

Three typos on the old page

The printed list says the midpoints of AC, AB, BD, AD, which does not produce a rhombus; the code uses AC, BD, AB, CD. The page also calls triangle KMN equilateral, but at the starting position KM and KN are short while MN is long: the equilateral half is KLM. Finally, it names bases CD and BC for the midlines, where the sides in the code are BC and AD. The test asserts what is true and reports all three differences.

Try "Construction" to see the eight midlines and the two equal sides, then drag C past B: the shared length turns negative, D flips to the other side of A, and the rhombus survives.
